name: Bilal Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Kessler and Sons. Family firm, builds four or five houses a year in the villages round here, proper detached houses on big plots. I'm lead carpenter, so I run the framing and the roofs, me and two others. Put it this way, I'm usually the first car in the yard at seven and the last one to lock the shipping container. I write the day's jobs in a paper diary, the same kind my dad used.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a frame's up and you stand in the middle of what'll be someone's kitchen and you can see the whole house. Mr Kessler still comes out and pats the timber like it's a horse. What wears me out is the drive, forty minutes each way on back roads, and the pay. Kessler's are fair people but they're small, they can't pay what the big firms pay. And there's no big firms out here anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much, to be honest. Maybe something like, there you go, still need people to build houses. I'm not really on social media, so it'd be a chat at the burger van at most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me. Which is fine. I'm not rich, but I know what Monday looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Same job, same crew, same diary. Maybe ask Mr Kessler about a bit more money in the spring, like I do every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I don't really get worked up about stuff I can't see on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI at all. Has anyone at Kessler's tried to get you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His grandson, Tom, does the office now, and he's got some program for quotes. He showed me once. I said that's lovely, Tom, and went back to my saw. I'm not against it, it's just not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, is there anything that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, I suppose. I've got about three weeks put by, because I helped my sister with her nursing course fees last year. If the van broke I'd be in trouble. But that's not an AI thing, that's a life thing.

S0.say: I'd say not much: there you go, you still need people to build houses. It'd be a chat at the burger van at most, since I'm not really online.
S0.think: It means nothing changes for me, which is fine. I'm not rich, but I know what Monday looks like.
S0.do: Keeps going with the same job, crew and paper diary. Asks his boss for a bit more money in the spring, as he does every year.
S0.feel: Calm, since he doesn't get worked up about things he can't see on site.
S0.quote: I said that's lovely, Tom, and went back to my saw.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal is unhurried and practical, with a strong attachment to routine and a family firm he trusts. He is not hostile to technology, just uninterested. His money is thin partly because he paid towards his sister's course fees, which says something about him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some of it will be useful and some of it won't, and we'll see. You get these waves of new stuff. Some of it sticks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think a small builder out here will be one of the last places it reaches. That's good for me in the short run. In the long run, if the big firms build houses cheaper with machines, Kessler's has to keep up or shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep my eyes open. If Kessler's buys some new kit, I'll learn it then, when I have to. Maybe I'd try to put fifty a month away, just in case. I wouldn't go chasing courses on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not losing sleep. Just a little thing in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kessler's would be slow to change. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not sure. Tom's young and keen. If he decides the factory panels are cheaper, we'll be standing them up instead of building them. Mr Kessler won't be in charge forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take to get you to try something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work on our job. Not on a video, on our plot, with our weather. If it saves a day and doesn't fall apart, fine. I'm stubborn, not stupid.

S1.say: I'd say some of it will be useful and some won't, and we'll see. New things come in waves and some of them stick.
S1.think: A small builder out here will be one of the last places it reaches, which helps me for now. But if big firms build cheaper with machines, Kessler's has to keep up or shut.
S1.do: Carries on and waits for his employer to bring in new kit before learning it. Tries to put about 50 a month aside, but would not chase courses on his own.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, a small worry at the back of his mind.
S1.fieldNote: Bilal sees both sides calmly: his rural family firm buys him time, but the boss's grandson could change things. He will learn only when the job requires it. He is honest that his stubbornness is a choice he would drop if shown proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's ready, which is just true. I wouldn't be marching, that's not me. But I'd say the government needs to sort something out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be in real trouble. Three weeks of money, a forty-minute drive to the nearest anything, and the only thing I know how to do is the thing the robot does. I don't know where I'd start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, cut back. Sell the second-hand quad bike I barely use, stop eating out, cancel the gym I never go to. If it got bad, I'd give up the flat and move back in with my mum, she's got a spare room. And I'd look for anything local, handyman work, fixing things for old people in the villages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying there at night thinking about it, which I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back in with your mum. How would that actually go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be over the moon, to be honest, and I'd hate it. She'd make my packed lunch like I'm fifteen. But it's free, and she's on her own, so maybe I'd be useful. Family's there for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What else could you do round here, if the building work went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The farm, maybe, but farms will have robots too. Fixing things in old houses, people's gates and back doors, maybe. Old folk in the villages like a face they know. That might last a bit longer.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and nobody's ready, which is just true. I wouldn't march, but the government needs to sort something out.
S2.think: I'd be in real trouble: three weeks of money, forty minutes from anything, and the only thing I know is what the robot does. I wouldn't know where to start.
S2.do: Cuts back by selling his quad bike and cancelling the gym and eating out. Gives up his flat to move into his mother's spare room if needed, and looks for local handyman work for older villagers.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake, which he says he never does.
S2.quote: She'd make my packed lunch like I'm fifteen.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture is the first time Bilal's calm cracks. His safety net is family, his mother's spare room, which he accepts with humour and some embarrassment. His fallback is small local repair work for people who want a familiar face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got some time, so people should plan. Not panic, plan. I'd say the same thing to the others at football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still bad for me, but I'd have time to get a bit of money together first. That's the main thing, a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe a hundred a month if I cut the quad bike and the eating out early. Carry on at Kessler's while it lasts. Probably wait and see what the robots actually look like on a site before I do anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a storm you can see coming over the hills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably wait. Five years, though. What would get you moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first one on a real job nearby. Once I've seen it, I'll know what I'm up against. Until then I'd just be guessing, and I don't like spending money on guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to Mr Kessler about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I would. He'd tell me straight. He's been through recessions, he'd know if the firm could last. If he said it's over, I'd believe him and start looking.

S3.say: I'd say we have some time, so people should plan, not panic. I'd say the same thing at football.
S3.think: It's still bad for me, but I'd have time to get some money together first. A cushion is the main thing.
S3.do: Saves harder, aiming for about 100 a month by cutting back early. Stays at Kessler's while it lasts and waits to see robots on a real site before making any bigger move.
S3.feel: Anxious, like watching a storm coming over the hills.
S3.quote: I don't like spending money on guesses.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Bilal's instinct is to save and wait for proof. He trusts his boss's judgement more than any news story. He would act only once he had seen a robot on a nearby site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen. I'd probably not say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel it's a problem for later. Which is maybe the wrong way to think, but that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Kessler's. Keep saving what I can. Maybe in five or six years, once it's clearer, look at what jobs are still around and see if I need a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-seven. Would you still be at Kessler's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they're still going, yes. Tom might have taken over by then. I'd like to still be building roofs at thirty-seven, I'm not ready to be a man who watches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying wait. Is there a risk you wait too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Probably. My dad waited too long on lots of things. But I'd rather wait and be sure than jump and break my leg. I'll take my chances.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and a lot can happen. I probably wouldn't say much more than that to anyone.
S4.think: I'd feel it's a problem for later. That might be the wrong way to think, but that's how I am.
S4.do: Carries on at Kessler's and keeps saving what he can. Waits five or six years, until things are clearer, before looking at which jobs remain and whether he needs a course.
S4.feel: Uneasy, with the change there but a long way off.
S4.quote: I'd rather wait and be sure than jump and break my leg.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture lets Bilal settle back into routine. He admits he may wait too long, as his father did, and accepts that risk. His pride in hands-on work comes through in not wanting to be "a man who watches".

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time, no money, nowhere to go. What would help? Some money coming in while you work out the next thing, so you're not rushing into anything stupid. And maybe somebody local you can talk to, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe ask about the small firms. Everyone thinks about the big building companies. But places like Kessler's are what keeps villages going. If they go, it's not just jobs, it's who fixes your roof when it leaks.

headlineQuote: I'd like to still be building roofs at thirty-seven, I'm not ready to be a man who watches.
portrait: Bilal is a 27-year-old lead carpenter for a small family house builder in the countryside, single, with about three weeks of savings after helping pay his sister's course fees. He keeps a paper diary, never uses AI and takes life as it comes. He stays calm or only uneasy in the slower pictures, trusting that a rural family firm will be the last to change, but AGI in two years leaves him alarmed, with his mother's spare room as his safety net. Given five or ten years he would save and wait for proof, knowing he might wait too long.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd be no time, no money and nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: Some income while he works out what to do next, and a local person to talk to rather than a website.
